title: Scientific Machine Learning-Based Climate-Adaptive Co-Design of Electric Bus Charging Infrastructure and Control
content: Electric bus operators must limit charging-infrastructure investment while supplying enough layover energy to preserve battery reserves during service. Climate changes both energy demand and charging acceptance, linking forecasts to control and infrastructure selection. We propose a scientific machine learning (SciML) framework for climate-adaptive co-design that predicts bus energy from an equipment-based physical prior and multimodal residual learning. Day-level calibration converts forecasts into upper energies that determine inventory targets and charging-window commitments; linear-programming screening is followed by closed-loop qualification of site sets. Public weather and reconstructed Montréal and Singapore duties drive continuous-year simulation with one vehicle configuration. With 28 target fitting days plus 40 calibration days, Singapore-to-Montréal transfer lowers 2025 forecast error by 5.4% against full fine-tuning and 18.7% against gradient boosting. Removing the physical prior and route-network inputs raises error 2.3 to 3.0 times. In 2025, reverse transfer lowers error by 58.0% against the calibrated physical prior and remains 11.3% above gradient boosting. Prediction accuracy and reserve outcomes rank the frozen predictors differently. On Singapore's eight-site design under fixed control in 2025, gradient boosting has the lowest forecast error but 135.03 lost days per operating seed, compared with 9.80 for transfer and 0.43 for the calibrated physical prior. Lost days count failures beyond a forecast-free full-site Reference plus uncommitted dates. Predictor-specific control pairing lowers transfer's lost days from 9.80 to 0.30. In Montréal, qualification restores the terminal needed on the coldest development day. The qualified eight-site predictive design lowers annual charging-subsystem cost by 28.2% against the full-site Reference.
